content: Mastitis in breastfeeding women can result from improper positioning of the infant at the breast or restricted feeding patterns. When mastitis is caused by an infection, the most common pathogen involved is Staphylococcus aureus. The condition is relatively common, with a prevalence rate of up to 33% among breastfeeding women. Standard treatment approaches typically include effective milk removal, the use of pain-relieving medications, and antibiotic therapy. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of antibiotic treatments in alleviating symptoms of mastitis in breastfeeding women, regardless of whether laboratory investigations were conducted to confirm the diagnosis. To gather relevant data, the researchers searched the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register up to September 30, 2012. They also contacted investigators and experts in the field to identify unpublished trials and reviewed the reference lists of retrieved articles. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that compared different types of antibiotic therapies or compared antibiotic therapy to alternative treatments for mastitis. Two authors independently assessed the quality of the trials and extracted data. In cases of disagreement, a third author was consulted to resolve disputes. Only two trials met the inclusion criteria for this review. One small trial, involving 25 participants, compared the effectiveness of amoxicillin and cephradine. The results showed no significant difference between the two antibiotics in terms of symptom relief or the prevention of abscess formation. Another, older study compared three approaches: breast emptying alone as a form of supportive therapy, antibiotic therapy combined with supportive therapy, and no treatment at all. This study suggested that women who received antibiotics experienced faster symptom resolution. However, the study's design had significant methodological flaws, which limit the reliability of its findings. The authors concluded that there is currently insufficient evidence to either confirm or refute the effectiveness of antibiotic therapy for treating lactational mastitis. They emphasized the urgent need for high-quality, double-blinded randomized controlled trials to determine whether antibiotics should be routinely used for this common postpartum condition.
